title: Mariska Hargitay nearly left 'Law & Order SVU' over fear of being a 'one-trick pony'
summary: Mariska Hargitay revealed she once told Julianna Margulies she needed to leave "SVU," but her blunt response changed everything.
story: Dennis Quaid spoke out about receiving the 2026 Patriot Ally Award at the 2nd Annual Military & Veteran Entertainment Awards Gala.
Mariska Hargitay once considered leaving "Law & Order: Special Victims Unit" after more than two decades as Olivia Benson because she worried the role had come to define her career.
In a new interview with Variety, the actress — who has starred as Benson since "SVU" premiered in 1999 — said she began questioning her future on the long-running NBC drama around its 25th season.
"I’ve got to leave the show too. I don’t want people to think I’m a one-trick pony," Hargitay recalled telling "ER" co-star Julianna Margulies.
'THE BIG BANG THEORY' STAR JIM PARSONS SAYS HE PAID A STEEP PRICE FOR FAME
Mariska Hargitay explained why she nearly quit "Law & Order: SVU" during a new interview with Variety. (Getty Images; Michael Schwartz for Variety)
Margulies, who famously left "ER" after six seasons, had a blunt response.
"Sweetheart, that ship’s sailed," Hargitay said Margulies told her.
While Benson made her a household name, the Emmy winner admitted she often felt constrained creatively due to the grueling production schedule.

"The comedy thing was painful to me because I felt like I was only exercising one part of myself," Hargitay said. "People would say, ‘You need to get off that show and do comedy. You need to get off that show and have a talk show.’"
‘X-FILES’ STAR GILLIAN ANDERSON REVEALS PARENTING REGRET, SAYS SHE WISHES SHE WAS 'LESS SELFISH'
Hargitay has portrayed Olivia Benson since 1999. (Jose Perez/Bauer-Griffin/GC Images)

"I wasn’t ready to leave, because I loved it," she said. "And then I got to do all this other stuff, and that’s why I don’t think about leaving right now. Do I want to quit now? No. Why? I made a movie while shooting; I did a play for six weeks on hiatus. I’m hosting the Emmys."
In 2023, Hargitay opened up to Fox News Digital about franchise creator and producer Dick Wolf's "great writing."

"Dick Wolf is truly a visionary," she said Tuesday. "And I think that's a very singular thing to be a true visionary who understands our culture in a very deep way, but also understands it's sort of ironic that a crime show would be actually calming in a way to our nervous system, knowing that somebody is out there taking care of it."
Mariska Hargitay said she's not thinking about leaving "SVU" anytime soon. (Michael Schwartz for Variety)
She continued, "That our voices are heard and there are people that are on it. So that is it."
MARISKA HARGITAY JOKES ABOUT BEING LONGTIME ‘LAW & ORDER’ CO-STAR CHRIS MELONI'S ‘SECOND WIFE’

"It's a very sort of interesting dichotomy," Hargitay added. "Because you think about a crime show, which normally should sort of upset your nervous system, actually can settle it down because of that."
"Law & Order's" success spawned seven spinoffs, including "Special Victims Unit," "Criminal Intent," "Trial by Jury," "LA," "UK," "True Crime" and "Organized Crime."

The actress is gearing up to host the Emmys next month. (Nathan Congleton/NBC via Getty Images)

In 2019, "SVU" became the longest-running live-action television series in history. Hargitay has starred as Detective Olivia Benson in the police procedural since its premiere in 1999 and became an executive producer in 2016.

title: John Candy's family calls out Hollywood for weight criticism the actor endured throughout his career
summary: Jennifer Candy-Sullivan and Rosemary Candy slam Hollywood's weight criticism of John Candy, revealing how the late comedian handled it privately.
story: The legendary actor's wife and daughter told Fox News Digital the focus on his weight was "upsetting," but that he handled it well.
John Candy's family is calling out Hollywood for how their father was treated.

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital at Televerse 26, the late actor's daughter, Jennifer Candy-Sullivan, and her mother, Rosemary Candy, slammed Hollywood for the way their father's weight was discussed during his fame.

"I think everyone who had some sort of difference was kind of put under a magnifying glass. So for him, it was his weight. And he kind of... he took it like a gentleman," Jennifer said. "And I think as his career went on, he was able to be more comfortable with himself and kind of vocalize and speak up for himself."

She went on to say that because of his career, people "thought he was the everyday guy and everyone loved him," so it would be okay to "pal around" and "joke around him," but that "in reality, it wasn't that okay. It was not cool."
John Candy's daughter and widow slammed Hollywood for the way they spoke about his weight during his fame. (Robin L Marshall/Getty Images; Steve Schapiro/Corbis via Getty Images)

Jennifer doesn't think the public or the media would be any less harsh on her father if his rise to fame occurred today, saying, "I think there would be a different type of kind of critique to him."

"I think if he tried losing weight, then it would be like, 'You're too skinny, you're no longer funny.' So I think Hollywood would find something," she said. "It would be... he doesn't... he would do something wrong. Ultimately, I think anyone in Hollywood does something wrong."

title: 'Harry Potter' star Jessie Cave felt 'it was embarrassing' turning to OnlyFans amid money struggles

"Harry Potter" star Jessie Cave admitted she felt embarrassed about joining OnlyFans after struggling to support her four children despite appearing in the blockbuster film franchise.

During a Thursday appearance on ITV's "This Morning," Cave, who played Lavender Brown in the "Harry Potter" movies, said she faced financial pressure while raising four children and navigating an unpredictable acting career before joining the subscription-based platform.
"I was in Harry Potter, but it was a smallish part, and it was 20 years ago. I've done little roles ever since, and I've mainly done comedy," Cave said.
FORMER NICKELODEON CHILD STAR REVEALS HIDDEN PRICE OF FAME AFTER SHARING RESIDUAL CHECKS WORTH PENNIES

"Harry Potter" star Jessie Cave opened up about why she found it "embarrassing" to join OnlyFans. (Warner Bros./courtesy Everett Collection; Dave Benett/Getty Images)

Cave launched her account in March 2025 to post videos of herself brushing, braiding and styling her waist-length hair. She has described the content as catering to a niche audience with an interest or "fetish" in hair.

‘AMERICAN PIE’ ALUM SHANNON ELIZABETH TURNS TO ONLYFANS FOR ‘FRESH START’ AS DIVORCE UNFOLDS

"And I have done the odd job here, and I have managed to keep afloat for 18 years, and it just came to a moment a couple of years ago where I was like 'Oh yeah, I don't really know what I would do' and this was an option. I'm now so glad, I'm so glad."
Jessie Cave first opened up about joining OnlyFans in March 2025, saying she would try it for a year. (Keith Mayhew/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)

JAIME PRESSLY ADMITS SHE THOUGHT ONLYFANS WAS 'PORN' BEFORE HER SURPRISE DEBUT ON THE PLATFORM

"I thought I’d make five grand, be on it for a few months, and it would buy me time to work out what we’re going to do," Cave said. "But it’s now been over a year and a half, and it’s genuinely saved our lives."

Jessie Cave has previously shared that she was inspired by Lily Allen and Kate Nash. (Mike Marsland/WireImage)
"Kate Nash has funded her tours with doing it. I just thought, ‘I mainly do one-woman shows with puppets’," Cave continued. "Yes, I was in 'Harry Potter' but I'm a struggling artist basically."

title: Shelley Fabares, star of 'The Donna Reed Show' and 'Coach,' dead at 82
summary: Shelley Fabares starred on "The Donna Reed Show," hit No. 1 with "Johnny Angel" and earned two Emmy nods for "Coach" over a career spanning decades.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Shelley Fabares, the actress and singer who starred in "The Donna Reed Show" and earned two Emmy nominations for her role in "Coach," has died. She was 82.
Fabares died Saturday in Los Angeles surrounded by her loved ones, her family confirmed in a statement to the Associated Press. Her cause of death was not disclosed.

"To her family and friends, Shelley was a source of love, strength, laughter, and comfort," her family wrote, according to the outlet. "She had a remarkable ability to make people feel welcomed, valued, and cared for."
'GOMER PYLE: USMC' STAR RONNIE SCHELL DEAD AT 94 AFTER DECADES-LONG CAREER

"We will remember Shelley for her kindness, loyalty, wit, courage, and beautiful spirit. We will miss her deeply — not only as a celebrated performer, but as the loving and extraordinary person she was in our everyday lives," they added.
"The Donna Reed Show" star Shelley Fabares has died at the age of 82. (Mark Sullivan/WireImage; Harry Langdon/Getty Images)

Fabares became one of television's most recognizable young stars when she was cast as Mary Stone, the teenage daughter of the characters played by Donna Reed and Carl Betz, on "The Donna Reed Show" in 1958.
During her time on the hit family sitcom, Fabares unexpectedly launched a successful recording career after the show's producer, Tony Owen, decided to incorporate singing into the series.

The actress' debut single, "Johnny Angel," reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1962 and sold more than 1 million copies. She released several albums and scored additional hits with "Johnny Loves Me" and "The Things We Did Last Summer," though she later acknowledged that she never considered herself much of a singer.

Fabares left "The Donna Reed Show" as a regular cast member in 1963 but returned for guest appearances before the series ended in 1966. She remained close to Reed, whom she credited as a mentor who helped her navigate Hollywood as a young actress.

Donna Reed and Shelley Fabares are pictured with baseball player Don Drysdale of the Los Angeles Dodgers in an episode of "The Donna Reed Show." (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)
At the height of her teen idol fame, Fabares transitioned to the big screen and starred opposite Elvis Presley in three movies: "Girl Happy" in 1965, "Spinout" in 1966 and "Clambake" in 1967.
She also appeared in the 1964 surf movie "Ride the Wild Surf," the 1966 musical comedy "Hold On!" with Herman’s Hermits and the 1968 Hank Williams Jr. film "A Time to Sing."

Born Michele Ann Marie Fabares on Jan. 19, 1944, in Santa Monica, California, she was the niece of actress Nanette Fabray. Fabares began modeling as a young child and made her television debut at age 10 on an episode of "Letter to Loretta."

Her early credits included appearances in "The Bad Seed," "Never Say Goodbye," "Jeanne Eagels" and "Marjorie Morningstar." She also appeared with Annette Funicello in the 1958 Disney serial "Annette."

After her initial success as a teen star, Fabares built a prolific television career that spanned several decades. In 1971, she portrayed Joy Piccolo, the wife of Chicago Bears running back Brian Piccolo, whom James Caan played, in the acclaimed television movie "Brian's Song," which also starred Billy Dee Williams.
Elvis Presley and Shelley Fabares starred in the 1967 film "Clambake." (Getty Images)

Fabares later held regular roles on "The Brian Keith Show," "The Practice" and "Forever Fernwood." From 1978 to 1984, she played Francine Webster, the professional rival of Bonnie Franklin’s Ann Romano, on "One Day at a Time."
She also made guest appearances on television shows, including "The Twilight Zone," "Mannix," "The Rockford Files," "The Love Boat," "Fantasy Island," "Mork & Mindy" and "Murder, She Wrote."
MACKENZIE PHILLIPS SAYS SHE AND VALERIE BERTINELLI DRANK WINE, DID COCAINE DURING SITCOM BREAKS

In 1989, Fabares found renewed success when she joined the ABC sitcom "Coach" as Christine Armstrong, the girlfriend and eventual wife of Hayden Fox, the college football coach played by Craig T. Nelson.

Fabares remained with the series throughout its nine-season run, appearing with Craig T. Nelson, Jerry Van Dyke and Bill Fagerbakke until the show ended in 1997. Her performance earned her two Emmy nominations for Outstanding Supporting Actress in a Comedy Series, in 1993 and 1994.
'MIRACLE ON THE HUDSON' HERO CAPTAIN 'SULLY' SULLENBERGER REVEALS ALZHEIMER'S DIAGNOSIS
Shelley Fabares starred as Christine Armstrong on "Coach" from 1989 to 1997. (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

Later in her career, Fabares lent her voice to Martha Kent in several animated Superman projects, including "Superman: The Animated Series," "Justice League" and the 2006 film "Superman: Brainiac Attacks."

Fabares became an advocate for Alzheimer's awareness after her mother, Elsa, was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. She helped raise money for research, delivered speeches and testified before Congress about the disease. Her mother died in 1992.

In 1999, Fabares faced a serious health crisis when doctors discovered she had progressive liver failure related to autoimmune hepatitis. After spending nearly two years on a transplant waiting list, she had a liver transplant in October 2000.
Shelley Fabares remained married to "M*A*S*H" actor Mike Farrell for more than 40 years until her death. (Getty Images)

Fabares married record and film producer Lou Adler in 1964. The couple separated two years later, and their divorce was finalized in 1980.

title: Motown songwriter behind 'Money (That's What I Want)' and other hits dead at 87
summary: Janie Bradford Hobbs co-wrote "Money (That's What I Want)" with Berry Gordy and penned hits for Marvin Gaye, Stevie Wonder and The Supremes.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Janie Bradford Hobbs, an early Motown songwriter who co-wrote "Money (That’s What I Want)" and penned songs recorded by Marvin Gaye, Stevie Wonder and other music legends, has died after an extended illness at 87.
Bradford Hobbs died at a Los Angeles hospital, her family said Saturday.
Born in Charleston, Missouri, Bradford Hobbs later moved to Detroit, where neighbor and singer Jackie Wilson introduced her to Motown founder Berry Gordy in the late 1950s.
COMMODORES CO-FOUNDER AND FORMER BASSIST RONALD LAPREAD DEAD AT 75
Janie Bradford attends the Mary Wilson tribute at The GRAMMY Museum on March 4, 2022, in Los Angeles, California. (Emma McIntyre/Getty Images)

She started working for Motown as a receptionist in 1958, but her role soon went well beyond answering phones. Like many employees in Motown’s early days, Bradford Hobbs became involved in making the music.
She and Gordy wrote "Money (That’s What I Want)," which Barrett Strong recorded in 1959. The song became one of Motown’s first hits and was later recorded by The Beatles.

Bradford Hobbs also wrote "Too Busy Thinking About My Baby." The Temptations recorded the song first, and Marvin Gaye later had a hit with it. She also wrote songs for Stevie Wonder, The Supremes, Martha & The Vandellas and others.
Janie Bradford, left, and George Clinton attend a ceremony honoring Clinton with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, Jan. 19, 2024, in Los Angeles. (Richard Shotwell/Invision/AP, File)
"Janie was there with me from the very beginning, before there was even a Motown, and she will always hold a very special place in my heart and in the Motown family," Gordy said in a statement.
COUNTRY MUSIC ICON DON SCHLITZ, WHO WROTE KENNY ROGERS' HIT 'THE GAMBLER,' DEAD AT 73
Gordy described Bradford Hobbs as one of the people who believed in Motown before anyone knew what it would become.

"Janie was one of a special group I have always thought of as the original Motown family — the unsung heroes who believed in the dream before anyone knew what Motown would become," Gordy continued. "She was one of the people who helped make Motown what it became."
Janie Bradford attends The Paley Center For Media Hosts A Legendary Evening With Mary Wilson at The Paley Center for Media on Feb. 25, 2019 in Beverly Hills, California. (Leon Bennett/Getty Images)

Bradford Hobbs later became head of Writer Relations for Jobete, Motown’s publishing company. After leaving Motown, she founded the annual Heroes and Legends Awards, which honored figures in the music industry and awarded scholarships for about 30 years, according to her family.

She is survived by her husband, Wardean Hobbs; daughter, Nicole Hobbs; son, Lance Finney; and two grandsons. Funeral arrangements have not been completed.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

summary: Former Prince Andrew reportedly feels "abandoned" by the royal family after rejecting King Charles III's invitation to Balmoral, fearing outcast treatment.
story: Andrew Lownie, author of "Entitled," argues Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor worsened his own crisis and believes new Epstein-related details could still emerge.
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor reportedly feels "abandoned" by his family as his royal exile deepens.
British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard told Fox News Digital that friends are reportedly checking in regularly on the former Duke of York and "he's certainly not hiding away" from them.

In 2022, he was stripped of his military titles and patronages by his mother, the late Queen Elizabeth II, as he faced Epstein survivor Virginia Giuffre's sexual assault lawsuit against him. Andrew and Giuffre settled out of court for an undisclosed sum that year.
Giuffre died in April 2025.

Virginia Roberts holds a photo of herself at age 16, when she says Palm Beach multimillionaire Jeffrey Epstein began abusing her sexually. (Emily Michot/Miami Herald/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

In October 2025, King Charles III stripped his younger brother's royal titles as Andrew faced renewed scrutiny over his ties to Epstein. The scrutiny intensified following the publication of Giuffre's posthumous memoir and the release of documents detailing Andrew's relationship with Epstein.

On Feb. 19, Andrew was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office over an allegation that he shared confidential information with Epstein during his time as a U.K. trade envoy. He was released after being held for 11 hours in police custody. The investigation remains ongoing.

Andrew's friend told The Sun that the disgraced ex-duke rejected the king's invitation to Balmoral Castle because he feared he would be treated as an "outcast."

Every summer, the royal family gathers at Balmoral to spend time together privately. About 30 family members are expected to join the king for the traditional gathering this year. title: Hayden Panettiere's 'Guiding Light' co-star Beth Chamberlin says she believed actress would overcome troubles
summary: Beth Chamberlin recalls her special bond with Hayden Panettiere on "Guiding Light" and why she believed the actress would overcome her troubled times.
story: Beth Chamberlin details 'strong bond' with Hayden Panettiere

Hayden Panettiere’s former "Guiding Light" co-star Beth Chamberlin believed the actress would overcome the "troubled times" she faced and emerge as an even stronger performer before her sudden death at 36.

In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, Chamberlin — who starred as Panettiere’s on-screen mom on the 90s soap opera — opened up about her "special bond" with the late child star and the resilience she saw in her through difficult times.

"When I would hear about some of the troubled times that she was going through, I would think to myself, ‘She’s gonna get through this, and watch out world,’" Chamberlin told Fox News Digital. "Because when she gets through this, you are going to see some work on screen. You’re going to see things like you’ve never seen. I know Viola Davis made a comment that she is waiting to see what Hayden was going to fully become. And I think that puts it best because I think, that's how I was feeling too."
HAYDEN PANETTIERE DEAD AT 36
Beth Chamberlin, who starred as Hayden Panettiere's mom in "Guiding Light," opened up about her "special bond" with the late actress. (Getty Images; Everett Collection)
The "Heroes" and "Nashville" star was found dead inside a Greenville, South Carolina residence on Aug. 16.

Panettiere’s on-and-off boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, and his brother, Zach, called 911 after finding the actress unresponsive, according to a police report obtained by Fox News Digital. Hickerson later gave authorities a bag containing medication Panettiere had allegedly been taking.
POLICE SHOW UP AT HOME LINKED TO HAYDEN PANETTIERE’S ON-AND-OFF BOYFRIEND DAYS AFTER HER SUDDEN DEATH
Panettiere’s mother, Lesley Vogel, publicly raised questions about Brian’s role in her daughter’s life and death.

"Although my daughter and I were estranged, it was not for lack of care or love," she said in a statement to Entertainment Tonight. "It was due to the involvement of a toxic individual who I believe led to her death."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"Hayden was a beautiful and talented young woman who unfortunately became involved with the wrong person, and although her family tried to extricate him from her life, we were unable to be successful."⁠
Hayden Panettiere died on Aug. 16. She was 36.  (Getty Images)

Preliminary autopsy results found no signs of trauma that contributed to Panettiere’s death, the Greenville County Coroner's Office confirmed to Fox News Digital. However, Panettiere's death remains under investigation.
HAYDEN PANETTIERE REMEMBERED BY VIOLA DAVIS, BETHANY JOY LENZ AND OTHER CELEBRITIES AFTER SUDDEN DEATH AT 36
Fox News has learned the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) has also been contacted and is assisting with the investigation.
For Chamberlin, processing Panettiere’s death has been particularly difficult because she remembers her as the extraordinarily talented young girl she worked alongside on "Guiding Light."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
"She truly was just an amazing, amazing child actor," Chamberlin said. "You’ve never seen anything like it, actually."

"Acting requires a lot of work to create an emotional arc. Now in a soap opera, too, you have to remember everything's done in one take. It's a multi-camera shoot ... So you've got to get it right. And she was able to do that. With multiple pages, day after day."
DISNEY ALUM CHRISTY CARLSON ROMANO RIPS HOLLYWOOD FOR FAILING CHILD STARS AFTER HAYDEN PANETTIERE’S DEATH

Panettiere entered show business extraordinarily young, appearing in commercials as a baby before landing a role on "One Life to Live" at about 4 years old. Panettiere’s major breakthrough came as Claire Bennet, the seemingly indestructible cheerleader at the center of NBC’s superhero drama "Heroes," which ran from 2006 to 2010. She followed that success with another defining television role, country singer Juliette Barnes on "Nashville" from 2012 to 2018. (Getty Images)
Chamberlin says that while she has often discouraged children pursuing a career in acting, she strongly believed Panettiere was a special exception.

"I know there's so many people that will say, 'Oh, you shouldn't put children in the business' And I get that. And anybody that knows me, knows that when people in my life that have asked me, how about putting my kid in the businesses? I always say, 'Don't do it.' I didn't put my own kid in a business. But I've always maintained that Hayden was the exception to that. Because Hayden looked like she was in her element when she was there."
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Chamberlin said she hopes Panettiere will be remembered for her "extraordinary talent."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I really want people to remember her for the extraordinary talent she was. Because she truly was," she said. "As I've said before, I think she was the most talented child actor that ever walked on a set ... She was doing this astounding stuff on a soap opera in one take. And she was maybe doing 20 pages or 30 pages, 40 pages worth of scenes a day. That's a whole different animal. And so. That's what I would, I really want people to remember that, because that deserves to be set aside and held up."

title: Jill Wagner pitched Taylor Sheridan 'Lioness' after military husband revealed real-life program: What to know
summary: Jill Wagner pitched Taylor Sheridan the idea for "Lioness" after her husband David Lemanowicz, a U.S. Army major, introduced her to the program.
story: Laysla De Oliveira and Jill Wagner told Fox News Digital how the third season of Taylor Sheridan's hit series will be different from the rest.
Jill Wagner has been in the industry for decades and stars in Taylor Sheridan's hit show, "Lioness."
Even though she moved to California early in her career to pursue acting, she has returned to her country roots and lives on her Tennessee farm with her husband and two daughters.

With season three of "Lioness" premiering earlier this month, Fox News Digital is taking a look at everything to know about Wagner's personal life, her military connection, how her husband inspired her role in the series and more.
Jill Wagner pitched Taylor Sheridan's "Lioness" series. (John Nacion/Variety via Getty Images)
Wagner portrays Bobby, the tough, highly skilled leader of the Lioness program's Quick Reaction Force (QRF).
WHAT TAYLOR SHERIDAN'S BIGGEST STARS REALLY THINK ABOUT WORKING WITH THE 'YELLOWSTONE' CREATOR

Wagner not only stars in Sheridan's hit series, she was the one who pitched him the idea. She told Parade in 2024 that Sheridan crafted the role as Bobby specifically for Wagner, and she serves as an executive producer on the show.
Jill Wagner stars as Bobby on "Lioness." (Lauren "Lo" Smith/Paramount+)

"Taylor Sheridan was my old acting coach, and I had access to him," she began. "Taylor writes in such an honest and raw way. I didn’t want this show to become Barbies with guns. I wanted it to represent the women I knew and respected in the military, and he’s done that brilliantly."
Wagner went on to explain that in order for her to really bring Bobby to life, she had to sit down and speak with her lionessess.

"At first, I didn’t understand who Bobby was. I still find things about her even right before we do a take. I have met and talked to several real-life lionesses while researching the show," she said. "I took all those personalities and mashed them all together; thus, we have ‘Bobby.'"
Wagner and David Lemanowicz's love story
Wagner and Lemanowicz first met when they were teenagers, but reconnected in Afghanistan while Lemanowicz was serving in the Air Force and Wagner was meeting troops during a USO tour.
David Lemanowicz and Jill Wagner tied the knot in 2017. (Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images)
"I hadn’t seen her in 17 years," Lemanowicz recalled during a 2016 Hallmark Home & Family episode.

"My boss told me to check out the event, and I look at the photo and said, ‘I think I know this girl.’ Lo and behold, I go to the chow event where she’s signing autographs, and I ask her if she’s from North Carolina. She says ‘yes.’ I say, ‘Little town outside of Greensboro?’ She says, ‘yes.’ I say, ‘Did you ever go to any North Carolina Monarchs hockey games?’ She says, ‘yes.’ I say, ‘Do you remember dating the goalie?'" he called.
ZOE SALDAÑA SAYS TAYLOR SHERIDAN 'REALLY SEES WOMEN' AS LIONESS SEASON THREE HITS PARAMOUNT+
At the time, Wagner and Lemanowicz were both in relationships and didn't take their connection further. They met again, a year later, in Los Angeles and were both single.
Jill Wagner lives in Tennessee with her family. (Getty Images)

"The day I came back from filming ‘Christmas Cookies,’ my girlfriends wanted to take me out to dinner," Wagner said in the same episode. "We were leaving (in Los Angeles)... and then I hear, ‘Jill!’ and David had just walked in the restaurant I was walking out of, and boom!"
They tied the knot the following year in 2017.
Wagner’s husband has a military background

Wagner's husband is a former professional hockey player who later pursued a military career. According to People, he joined the military after his hockey career ended in 2008 and became a lieutenant in the U.S. Army Reserve.
The outlet noted he was promoted to U.S. Army major in 2020.
Jill Wagner and David Lemanowicz in 2018. (Getty Images)
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
During Wagner's Parade interview, she explained that Lemanowicz was the one who introduced her to the lioness program.

"My husband, David [Lemanowicz], was the one who told me about the Lioness program. From that moment on, I knew there was a story to tell. It took about five years, but I never gave up," she told the outlet in 2024.
Wagner comes from a military family
Wagner previously told Parade that she was raised in a military family.

"My grandfather, my uncle and my father were all Marines," she began. "My husband currently serves in the Army. I come from a very patriotic family, and I’ve always greatly respected the men and women who serve our country."
Jill Wagner as Bobby in "Lioness" season 3. (Emerson Miller/Paramount+)
She told the outlet that, given her background, she was intrigued to star in a show that portrayed women in the military in lead roles.

"I have not seen women in the military portrayed in lead roles like this. It is important to give these women the moment they deserve on screen while not taking any away from the men who also serve. They both deserve our respect for the sacrifices they make," Wagner said.
Wagner's "Lioness" character always has a toothpick in her mouth – which she told the outlet was homage to her father.
Wagner, Lemanowicz and their two daughters live on a Tennessee farm
Wagner left Los Angeles in 2016 after finding a farmhouse in Tennessee that she previously told People "looked like a scary haunted house" at first.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
When they purchased the home, Lemanowicz and Wagner were engaged and were planning on having a family.
Jill Wagner and David Lemanowicz kissing at the "Lioness" season 2 premiere. (Variety via Getty Images)
"We wanted a family, and I saw my children running around in the front yard. I knew it could be fixed. And I wanted to be the one to restore this piece of history," she said.
'LIONESS' STAR JILL WAGNER CHOSE TENNESSEE FARM LIFE TO RAISE HER FAMILY
Lemanowicz and Wagner share two daughters: Army Gray Lemanowicz, 6, and Daisy Roberta Lemanowicz, 5.
During an interview with Fox News Digital, Wagner explained that her decision to put roots down in Tennessee was an easy choice given her background.

title: Tom Hanks put 'Band of Brothers' stars in their place during boot camp 'mutiny,' Neal McDonough reveals
summary: Neal McDonough reveals how Tom Hanks arrived by helicopter to deliver a powerful speech that ended a cast mutiny during "Band of Brothers" boot camp.
story: "Band of Brothers" star Neal McDonough recalled how Tom Hanks unexpectedly arrived at boot camp and reminded the actors what they owed the real-life heroes of Easy Company.
"Band of Brothers" star Neal McDonough recalled how Tom Hanks put the show's cast in their place during the grueling boot camp that they underwent prior to filming.
McDonough, 60, co-starred in the hit 2001 HBO war drama miniseries, which was executive produced by Hanks, 70, and Steven Spielberg, 79.

"Band of Brothers" told the story of the real-life soldiers of Easy Company, part of the U.S. Army’s 506th Parachute Infantry Regiment, 101st Airborne Division, as they fought their way across Europe during World War II.
NEAL MCDONOUGH SAYS HOLLYWOOD LABELED HIM A ‘RELIGIOUS NUT,’ COST HIM HIS CAREER AND HOME

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, McDonough recalled how the actors rebelled during the production's intense boot camp before Hanks arrived by helicopter and delivered a powerful message that they "never forgot."
"About five days into boot camp, there was a mutiny," McDonough said on the red carpet at Televerse 26 in Los Angeles.
"Band of Brothers" star Neal McDonough recalled how Tom Hanks shut down a "mutiny" on the hit WWII drama's set. (Kate Green/Getty Images for The Walt Disney Company Limited; HBO via Getty Images)
"All of a sudden, my teeth are knocked out by a .30 cal and I broke my toe, and a slew of other guys was getting tortured," he continued.
"The American guys really loved it," he added with a laugh. "But, there was this mutiny going on. They were like, 'This isn't what we signed up for.'"
TOM HANKS JOKINGLY SWIPES MS NOW'S VIEWERSHIP WHILE APPEARING LIVE ON-AIR WITH REPORTER

"All of a sudden, this helicopter shows up in the middle of our Army base and out walks Tom Hanks with his beard down here and his ‘Cast Away’ hair," McDonough recalled, referencing Hanks' starring role in the survival drama "Cast Away."
WATCH: Tom Hanks arrived by helicopter to confront ‘Band of Brothers’ boot camp ‘mutiny,’ co-star says

"And he got us all attention, and he says, ‘Look, we all owe it to everyone in Easy Company, and everyone in World War II, to work our hardest because they gave their lives for our freedoms. The least we can do is work our tails off to tell the truth as hard as we can so we give honor to those men and women,'" McDonough remembered of Hanks.
McDonough told Fox News Digital that the two-time Oscar winner's words completely shifted the cast's mindset toward portraying "Band of Brothers'" real-life heroes.
"Telling you after that, we were all brainwashed," he said before clarifying, "I'm not sure brainwashed is the right word."
McDonough recalled how a powerful speech from Hanks completely changed the cast's outlook during their intense boot camp. (Getty Images)
STEVEN SPIELBERG ADMITS HE'S BEEN CONVERTED ON UFOS, SAYS HE BELIEVES THE BELIEVERS

"Where we all realized Tom was right," McDonough continued. "They lived, breathed, and died for what we have this day, freedom. None of us forgot about that, and as soon as the show came out, we realized Tom was right the whole time."

"He knew it was going to be a massive hit. Stephen knew it would be a big hit. We were just lughead actors who were doing our jobs. And then when it came out, and it was the hit that it became, and it is still 25 years later, it just boggles my mind how fortunate every single one of us were to be cast in the show."
ADRENALINE-PACKED PREVIEW RELEASED FOR UPCOMING D-DAY FILM 'PRESSURE,' FEATURES LOADED CAST

McDonough played 1st Lt. Lynn "Buck" Compton, a real-life platoon leader in Easy Company. Compton fought in major WWII campaigns, including D-Day and Operation Market Garden and was wounded during fighting in the Netherlands.
"Band of Brothers" told the story of the real-life war heroes of Easy Company.  (Getty Images)

"Band of Brothers" also starred Damian Lewis, Ron Livingston, Donnie Wahlberg, David Schwimmer, Michael Cudlitz and Scott Grimes, while future stars including Tom Hardy, Michael Fassbender and James McAvoy appeared in smaller roles.

The 10-part miniseries was based on historian Stephen E. Ambrose’s 1992 nonfiction book, "Band of Brothers" and was created by Hanks and Spielberg, who had previously collaborated on the acclaimed 1998 World War II film "Saving Private Ryan." Writer Erik Jendresen also helped lead the series adaptation.
Hanks also directed episode five, titled "Crossroads," and had a brief, uncredited cameo.
MATT DAMON WAS 'PUSHED TO THE LIMIT' WHILE FILMING 'THE ODYSSEY,' DETAILS GRUELING PHYSICAL DISCOMFORTS
"Band of Brothers," which premiered in September 2001, earned widespread critical acclaim and received multiple awards, including seven Emmys and a Golden Globe.

The series was extensively praised for its gritty realism and attention to historical detail. The boot camp that the actors underwent was specifically intended to help them move, behave and bond more convincingly as soldiers.
WATCH: Neal McDonough went to hospital as his ‘Band of Brothers’ character after brutal boot camp injury

While speaking with Fox News Digital, McDonough recalled how the "brutal" boot camp was led by Dale Dye, retired U.S. Marine Corps captain, Vietnam War veteran, actor and longtime Hollywood military technical advisor.
McDonough explained that the boot camp was more challenging for some actors than others.
"I'm a knucklehead. I love that kind of stuff. Those two weeks felt like three months for a lot of guys," he said. "And it was tough."
McDonough told Fox News Digital that Dale intentionally "allowed himself to be the common enemy" to the actors during the series' production.

"We all hated his guts, because he pushed us all to the brink," he recalled of Dye. "And it wasn't until about a quarter of the way through filming that we realized he was putting on an act so we could all gel together as a unit."

"There are a few men on this planet that I love like I love Dale Dye because he allowed himself to be that guy and 'Band of Brothers' would not be ‘Band of Brothers’ were not for him,'" McDonough added.
"Band of Brothers" military advisor and actor Dale Dye is pictured at the show's premiere in 2001. (WireImage)

In additional to serving as the senior military advisor for "Band of Brothers," Dye also played Col. Robert F. Sink, the real-life commander of the 506th Parachute Infantry Regiment, in the series. Dye is one of Hollywood’s leading military advisors and has previously worked on movies, including "Platoon" and "Saving Private Ryan," and TV shows, including "The Pacific" and "Masters of the Air."

Despite the cast's eventual gratitude for Dye's dedication and methods, the physically demanding boot camp took a toll on the actors. McDonough recalled that Dye even considered suspending the training after several actors suffered injuries. The "Minority Report" star remembered that he was hit in the mouth with a ".30 cal" shortly after.

"I heard him say, ‘If one more guy gets hurt, then I might shut this whole thing down.’ That afternoon, I got hit," McDonough said. "We're enveloping this one house. Guy comes out with a .30 cal, boom, smashes my teeth, blood all the way down here."
McDonough remembered that his co-star Shane Taylor, who played medic Eugene "Doc" Roe, became incredulous when he asked him for medical treatment after the injury.
"I said, ‘Doc, get over here, stitch me up,'" McDonough said.
McDonough recalled how he suffered a serious injury to his mouth during boot camp. (Getty Images)
McDonough recalled Taylor replying, "'I'm not a doctor, I'm an actor,'" to which he said he responded, "'I don't care, just stitch me up.'"

"So he stitches me up in front of everybody, and then two or three days later, it's so infected, that Dale's like, ‘You need to go to the hospital.’ And I knew he was sweating," McDonough said. "But at the time, I was just gung ho, because of what Tom said."
McDonough recalled that he went to the hospital, where he provided his character's name and information instead of his own.
"I knew it was socialized medicine, I knew. But I needed to have ‘Lynn Compton’ on that report, not ‘Neal McDonough,’" he said.
McDonough told Fox News Digital that the doctor who treated him was horrified when he saw his infected mouth.
"The doctor's like, 'Oh gosh, that's awful, this is terrible,'" he recalled. "So they shaved it all off, they cleaned it up, stitched me up."
WATCH: ‘Band of Brothers’ stars ‘hated’ boot camp leader before discovering it was all an act, Neal McDonough says

The "Yellowstone" alum told Fox News Digital that he visited Dye afterward. He remembered Dye becoming emotional when presented with McDonough's hospital paperwork, realizing how deeply the actor had committed to his portrayal of Compton.

"I get back to the barracks at 4 o'clock in the morning, I knock on his door, he's sitting there waiting. I put it down there [and said] ‘Sir.’ And he looks at it, and he looked at me and tears welled up in Dale's eyes," McDonough said.

"And I knew that I did a right thing for Easy Company and the whole movie, and after that, we became like that," he continued. "But that was probably the most difficult moment of the boot camp for me."
"Band of Brothers" was executive produced by Tom Hanks and Steven Spielberg. (FilmMagic, Inc)

McDonough met the real Compton prior to filming the show and the two developed a friendship that lasted until the former soldier's death in 2012. He previously described Compton as "another father figure" in his life, and said he nicknamed his son Morgan "Little Buck" in Compton’s honor. McDonough also attended Compton’s 90th birthday celebration and later gave a eulogy at his funeral.

While speaking with Fox News Digital, McDonough explained that "Band of Brothers" also had a special place in his heart because he met his longtime wife Ruvé Robertson while filming the show in the United Kingdom.
McDonough met his longtime wife Ruvé Robertson while filming the show in the United Kingdom. (Paul Archuleta/Getty Images)

McDonough and the South African model married in 2003 and share five children, Morgan, Catherine, London, Clover and James.

"The greatest thing about ‘Band of Brothers’ other than getting to play Buck Compton and work for Steven Spielberg and Tom Hanks, is I got to meet the love of my life, Ruvé, the very first night I got into town on St. Patrick's Day, 2000," he said. "Five kids later, 26 seasons later, I love her more today than I did yesterday and I love her tomorrow more than I did today."

title: Prince William, Harry’s former royal mentor reveals mother’s secret MI5 past after decades of silence
summary: Jamie Lowther-Pinkerton's novel draws on his mother's hidden MI5 intelligence work, her Auxiliary Territorial Service days and guarded secrets.
story: Jamie Lowther-Pinkerton reveals how his mother Sue’s remarkable life inspired his debut novel, "Beyond the Edge of Light."
Jamie Lowther-Pinkerton grew up knowing his mother had led an "amazing life." But there was one chapter she rarely spoke about.
After World War II, Sue Lowther-Pinkerton joined MI5 and worked in British intelligence during the Cold War. But she revealed little to her children about that part of her past.
Decades ago, while watching a documentary with her children, Sue let something slip.
KATE MIDDLETON SCALES UK'S THREE HIGHEST PEAKS IN 24 HOURS WITH A DEEPLY PERSONAL MESSAGE FOR CANCER SURVIVORS

Prince Harry, Private Secretary Jamie Lowther-Pinkerton and Prince William at the 10th anniversary memorial service for Diana, Princess of Wales at Guards Chapel at Wellington Barracks on Aug. 31, 2007, in London. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

"We were watching a documentary one afternoon about 30, 40 years ago," Lowther-Pinkerton recalled to Fox News Digital. "And there was a thing called the ‘Cambridge spy ring,’ which were Soviet agents who had infiltrated the British system. And there was a great mystery about who the fifth man was. And up pops the documentary maker saying, ‘Well, it could be Sir Roger Hollis.’"
Jamie Lowther-Pinkerton stands behind Prince William during a Remembrance Day service at Camp Bastion in southern Afghanistan. (PA Images via Getty Images)

Hollis served as director general of MI5 from 1956 to 1965. He later became the subject of allegations that he had secretly worked for the Soviet Union, claims that were investigated but never proven.
Sue didn't hesitate.
WATCH: PRINCE WILLIAM, HARRY’S FORMER ROYAL AIDE REVEALS MOTHER'S SECRET PAST
"My mother, without missing a knitting stitch, said, ‘Absolute nonsense. He was a total gentleman and a patriot.’"

"[My sister and I] both looked at her sideways as if she was completely mad," Lowther-Pinkerton said. "I tried to get more out of her, but she was of that generation who quite rightly just didn’t want to talk about it."
Sue Lowther-Pinkerton died on Dec. 24, 2023. (Courtesy of Jamie Lowther-Pinkerton)
Lowther-Pinkerton said he was in his mid-20s before he and his older sister learned of their mother's intelligence career.
"Beyond the Edge of Light" by Jamie Lowther-Pinkerton is available now. (Penguin Random House)

MI5, formally known as the Security Service, is Britain's domestic intelligence agency. According to MI5's official history, the agency traces its origins to the Secret Service Bureau, established in 1909. The bureau was later divided into domestic and foreign sections that developed into MI5 and MI6.

That rare glimpse into his mother's past stayed with Lowther-Pinkerton for decades. Now, her extraordinary life has helped inspire his novel, "Beyond the Edge of Light," a wartime love story. Its central character, Missie, a rebellious young woman who joins military intelligence, was inspired by Sue, who died in 2023 at age 99.
Jamie Lowther-Pinkerton. (Courtesy of Jamie Lowther-Pinkerton)
Long before Sue entered the secretive world of MI5, she had already lived a life of adventure.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
ATS women take a break at a 3.7-inch anti-aircraft gun site at Wormwood Scrubs in London on Oct. 22, 1941. (Imperial War Museums via Getty Images)

As World War II unfolded, she worked on NAAFI (Navy, Army and Air Force Institutes) vans serving tea and food to troops and painted white lines on roads before she was old enough to enlist. In 1942, she joined the Auxiliary Territorial Service, the women’s branch of the British Army.
Princess Elizabeth, as junior commander in the ATS, inspects the Motor Transport Training Centre on May 1, 1945. (Mirrorpix via Getty Images)

She was later posted to the Royal School of Artillery at Larkhill, where she drove gun limbers — vehicles used to transport artillery equipment — across firing ranges. Because the work was considered dangerous, she received an additional four pence a day.
After the war, her work took her into an even more secret world.
Jamie Lowther-Pinkerton's late mother Sue. (Courtesy of Jamie Lowther-Pinkerton)

"She went into Secret Service," Lowther-Pinkerton said. "So she joined MI5, which was the equivalent. It's a sort of mixture between the FBI, I think, and the CIA. And she was in that during the Cold War."

Sue's intelligence career began even before she joined MI5. According to The Telegraph's obituary, she worked in Army intelligence in Singapore after leaving the military in 1948. There, she was entrusted with secret communications concerning HMS Amethyst's planned 1949 breakout from China's Yangtze River.
One of the secret MI5 files released for the first time to the Public Records Office in Kew, London. (PA Images via Getty Images)

After returning to Britain in 1951, Sue joined MI5 and worked at Leconfield House. But she remained fiercely guarded about what she did there — even with her son, who would go on to serve in the Irish Guards and the Special Air Service (SAS).
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Jamie Lowther-Pinkerton guided Prince William and Prince Harry through their entry into the armed forces. (Indigo/Getty Images)

Growing up, Lowther-Pinkerton heard stories of his mother being raised in India and eventually getting "kicked out of every educational establishment she ever went to." He described his mother, who didn’t see her parents for years on end, as "incredibly wild."

Sue received 11 marriage proposals before Lowther-Pinkerton’s father, Anthony Hull Lowther-Pinkerton, or "Rumpty," a "great big Anglo-Irishman" who was "everybody’s life and soul of the party," wooed her.
Jamie Lowther-Pinkerton attends the annual Chelsea Pensioners Founders Day Parade at Royal Hospital Chelsea on June 9, 2011, in London. (Indigo/Getty Images)

"[They] had all of us children and went to live in Suffolk, which is where I grew up," he said. "... [My father] could go up and down in moods. And my mother just ... kept the family going absolutely on the straight and narrow through the middle with her calmness really. That was the great thing about her. Nothing fazed her."

Kate Middleton attends the Sovereign's Parade at Sandhurst Military Academy in Surrey, England, on Dec. 15, 2006, accompanied by Prince William's private secretary Jamie Lowther-Pinkerton. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

"I remember one occasion when my father got really down in the dumps," he recalled. "She made really good roast potatoes for lunch. And she’d obviously had enough. She got this potato, and she flung it down the dining room table with [my sister] Sarah and me on either side thinking, ‘My goodness, what’s going to happen now?’

"And she hit my father clean between the eyes. My father was literally crying with laughter within about 20 seconds. She just knew. It wasn’t always roast potatoes, but she knew how to deal with him."

Prince Harry walks with his private secretary, Jamie Lowther-Pinkerton, after attending a service of morning prayer at Christ Church Cathedral on March 4, 2012, in Nassau, Bahamas. (John Stillwell-Pool/Getty Images)

According to Sue’s obituary, she remained in MI5 until leaving in 1956 to start a family. For almost 50 years, she helped organize the annual Poppy Appeal, a fundraising campaign supporting veterans, active-duty service members and their families. For several decades, she also delivered Meals on Wheels to remote cottages and farmsteads.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Queen Elizabeth II and Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother in 1990. (John Shelley Collection/Avalon/Getty Images)
Lowther-Pinkerton’s life also took an unexpected turn. He went on to serve in the royal household as an equerry to Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother.
"She was an absolute joy to be with," he said with a smile. "She was like everybody’s favorite granny. She had a bolt of steel running down her spine, so nothing fazed her."
Glamis Castle turrets in Forfar, Angus, Scotland. (Andrew Holt/Construction Photography/Avalon/Getty Images)

"She was the daughter of a Scottish girl who grew up in Glamis Castle. When she was 15, her favorite brother was killed in the trenches in the First World War. And Glamis Castle was given over, at least a part of it, to being a military hospital for wounded soldiers coming back from the First World War."

"Like my mother, she had an incredibly sharp memory," he continued. "I remember sitting with the Queen Mother at lunch and talking about the war. It was enlightening. And she had a wonderful sense of humor. I absolutely adored her."
WATCH: FORMER ROYAL AIDE RECALLS LESSON HE LEARNED FROM PRINCE WILLIAM

The gig came with perks. Lowther-Pinkerton laughed when reminded that he would mix the martinis for her parties. He previously told People magazine the drinks were seven parts gin with "a whiff of vermouth." According to the outlet, he would top her "decent-sized drink" with ice.

Prince William, left, and Prince Harry are greeted by Jamie Lowther-Pinkerton as they arrive for the unveiling of a statue of their mother, Princess Diana, at The Sunken Garden in Kensington Palace, London, on July 1, 2021, which would have been her 60th birthday. (Pool/AFP via Getty Images)

Lowther-Pinkerton served as a private secretary to Prince William, Prince Harry and later Kate Middleton, from 2005 to 2013, People reported. He served as a mentor for the princes. His son Billy was a page at William and Kate’s wedding.
The couple later asked Lowther-Pinkerton to be a godfather to their eldest son, Prince George.

Kate Middleton hands Jamie Lowther-Pinkerton bunches of flowers during a walkabout after attending the naming ceremony and service of dedication of the Atlantic 85 lifeboat Hereford Endeavour at Trearddur Bay Lifeboat Station at Anglesey on Feb. 24, 2011 in Bangor, Wales. (Indigo/Getty Images)
Lowther-Pinkerton said the remarkable women in his life have inevitably influenced his writing. "It all seeps in," he said.
His mother, however, remains at its heart.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Jamie Lowther-Pinkerton and Prince William watch the parade and flypast during the Battle of Britain 70th Anniversary Service at Westminster Abbey on Sept. 19, 2010, in London. (Indigo/Getty Images)
"Somebody of strength, somebody who has their own opinions and is not going to be pushed around," he said of the legacy he hopes Sue leaves with readers.
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: ‘Dukes of Hazzard’ star John Schneider admits he lied his way into iconic Bo Duke role at 18
summary: The Bo Duke actor revealed how he fabricated his age, hometown and driving credentials to win over "Dukes of Hazzard" producers in 1978.
story: The ‘Dukes of Hazzard’ star told Fox News Digital he was proud to be asked by the White House to perform for the nation's 250th anniversary.
John Schneider didn't exactly follow the traditional path to Hollywood stardom.
At just 18 years old, the New York native convinced producers of "The Dukes of Hazzard" he was a 24-year-old Georgia farm boy with racing experience.
Somehow, the gamble paid off.

"I told them, I said, 'Look, I'm 24 years old from Snailville, Georgia. I grew up on a farm, and I just came in first in my class at the Georgia School of High Performance Driving,' which did not exist. … You couldn't ask your phone if this place existed."
‘DUKES OF HAZZARD’ STAR JOHN SCHNEIDER BREAKS SILENCE ON EX-WIFE'S COURT BATTLE: 'EVERYTHING'S A NEGOTIATION'
John Schneider, as Bo Duke, in the made-for-television movie, "The Dukes of Hazzard: Reunion!" in 1997.  (CBS via Getty Images)
The wild confession came as Schneider looked back on his unlikely rise to television fame during an appearance on "Arroyo Grande with Raymond Arroyo."
"I learned a long time ago, you don't get a second chance to make a first impression," Schneider said. "I gave them exactly what I thought they wanted."
"Yeah, they were looking for good old boys from the rural South, 24 to 30, with no acting experience, but a lot of racing experience."
Schneider checked almost none of those boxes.
‘BRADY BUNCH’ STAR SHARES THE SIMPLE WORD THAT SAVED HER FROM HOLLYWOOD TRAPS
American actors John Schneider, Catherine Bach and Tom Wopat in a promotional portrait for the TV show "The Dukes of Hazzard," circa 1980. (Silver Screen Collection/Getty Images)
"And, of course, I was 18, from Westchester County, New York. … I've done theater for 10 years.
"Years later, I found out that one of the producers was — his opinion was, ‘Over my dead body is this hick going to have anything to do with my television show.’"
Another producer, however, saw something the first one didn't.
JOHN SCHNEIDER BLASTS CLAIMS THE AMERICAN FLAG IS A 'DIVISIVE SYMBOL': 'THESE PEOPLE ARE OUT OF THEIR MINDS'
"But the other one, thankfully, who had a little bit more juice, said, ‘That's him. That's Bo Duke.’
"He and I finally won that argument. … That was 1978."
American actors Tom Wopat and John Schneider in a promotional portrait for the TV show "The Dukes of Hazzard," circa 1980. (Getty Images)
Schneider's story was so audacious Arroyo had to ask the obvious question: Was it nerve or desperation?
"What's the difference?" Schneider laughed.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
For Schneider, it was neither.
"When the smoke clears, no … it was where preparation meets opportunity."
And the actor had already been studying Hollywood's biggest opportunities.
Actors Burt Reynolds and Sally Field in the film "Smokey and the Bandit." (Getty Images)
"You know, I recognized ‘Smokey and the Bandit’ had just beaten all the box office records in ’77 until ‘Star Wars’ came along."
But Schneider's connection to the Burt Reynolds classic was even more improbable.

He was living in Atlanta at the time and wanted to get onto the set.
"I was, but I wasn't supposed to be. … I acted, some people would say — or lied, some other people would say — my way onto that set as well."
Schneider laughed off the admission, explaining he has always operated with an expectation that something big could happen.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
John Schneider, left, Tom Wopat and Ben Jones on the TV series "The Dukes of Hazzard," circa 1983. (Getty Images)
"So, I guess … it was not desperation. It was just, I’ve always, for some reason, expected great opportunity every day."

"The Dukes of Hazzard" premiered in 1979 and followed "the fast-drivin’, rubber-burnin’ Duke boys of Hazzard County." The series ran for seven seasons and 147 episodes, becoming a massive Friday night ratings draw, at one point attracting as many as 40 million viewers.
Schneider went on to become synonymous with Bo Duke, later appearing in projects including "Smallville."

title: Hayden Panettiere's co-star Justin Chatwin 'p----- off' over Hollywood culture after her passing
summary: Justin Chatwin slammed Hollywood culture for failing people battling trauma and addiction as he grieves "Sleepwalker" co-star Hayden Panettiere.
story: Hayden Panettiere's preliminary autopsy results show no signs of trauma contributing to her death at age 36.
Justin Chatwin is "p----- off" over Hollywood culture as he grieves the death of "Sleepwalker" co-star Hayden Panettiere.

In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, Chatwin, who recently worked alongside Panettiere on what became her final film, said his grief has turned to anger over what he sees as a lack of support for people struggling with trauma and addiction in the entertainment industry.
"I'm a man, so I process things by getting p----- off," Chatwin said. "And so I'm kind of angry that this is the culture that and this is the industry that people aren't taken care of.
HAYDEN PANETTIERE AND THE CHILD STARS WHOSE RELATIONSHIPS WITH THEIR MOMAGERS TURNED COMPLICATED
Justin Chatwin, who starred with Hayden Panettiere in two films, spoke out after her death. (Getty Images)
"They get the work, they sell the product," he continued, "and there's just a lot of people in our industry that are dying from … inability to feel pain or heal trauma."
Chatwin added that "there's not enough support or awareness around these issues," before saying, "Yeah, I'm grieving."
Panettiere died Aug. 16, at the age of 36.

The "Heroes" and "Nashville" star was found in cardiac arrest at her home in Greenville, South Carolina, according to the Greenville County Coroner's Office. Emergency personnel attempted life-saving measures before Panettiere was pronounced dead. An autopsy found no signs of trauma that contributed to her death.
WLADIMIR KLITSCHKO MOURNS FORMER FIANCÉE HAYDEN PANETTIERE, VOWS TO KEEP HER MEMORY ALIVE FOR DAUGHTER KAYA
Panettiere died Aug. 16. She was 36.  (Emma McIntyre/Getty Images for amfAR)
Her official cause and manner of death have not yet been determined, and the investigation remains ongoing.
Chatwin said the struggles he witnessed extend far beyond Hollywood, describing trauma and addiction as an issue affecting people across the country.
"It's not just her," Chatwin said. "We've lost a lot of people, and not just Hollywood, in all of America. It's an epidemic that needs to be looked at."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Chatwin said his final time with Panettiere came after the two finished working together on "Sleepwalker," when they went out to dinner after the film's wrap.
"We went out to dinner after we wrapped the movie and, yeah, she was one of the top five, top 10 favorite people that I've ever worked with," he recalled. "She was super sweet."
Chatwin said Panettiere was one of his favorite actors to work with.  (Getty Images)
However, Chatwin said he could also sense that Panettiere was carrying significant pain.

"I could sense a lot of pain that she had dealt with, from her family to her daughter," he said. "I could sense the heaviness and the weight that the toll of 20 years in Hollywood and … trauma and the fight to figure out the trauma and addiction can have on you."
Panettiere had spoken publicly about her struggles with addiction and other personal challenges. She detailed many of those experiences in her 2026 memoir, "This Is Me: A Reckoning."
GOLDIE HAWN SOUNDS THE ALARM ON CHILDHOOD CELEBRITY CULTURE: 'ALL I CAN SAY IS IT'S A NIGHTMARE'

Chatwin first met Panettiere years earlier when she was in her 20s and starring on "Heroes." The two later reunited to work together on "Sleepwalker," a psychological thriller released in January. Panettiere starred as Sarah Pangborn, a grieving mother, and also served as an executive producer on the film.
"She's just got one of the biggest hearts of anyone that I've worked with," Chatwin said. "And she's super sweet."
But Chatwin said he noticed a difference in his co-star when they reunited.
"Life had taken a toll on her, and she had a lot of unfortunate incidents," he said.
The actor also opened up about the loneliness that can exist behind the glamour of Hollywood, describing the stark transition performers can experience when they leave a movie set.
Panettiere had been open about her struggles with addiction.  (Michael Buckner/Variety via Getty Images)

"Sometimes the pain is unbearable, and at the end of the day, you go home from a warm, fun movie set where everyone's telling you you're great, and you're alone in your house and you still got to order your coffee and eat your dinner," Chatwin said. "It's a really lonely career."
On set, however, Chatwin remembered Panettiere as "super fun" and said he treasured their deeper conversations.
"I really love having deep conversations with her," he said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Reflecting on Panettiere's experience while making "Sleepwalker," Chatwin also offered a warning to fellow performers about taking on roles that could force them to revisit unresolved experiences.
"I think that actors need to consider what roles they play, especially if it's opening up a vulnerable trauma that isn't healed," he said.

Panettiere rose to fame as a child actor before becoming widely known for playing cheerleader Claire Bennett on NBC's "Heroes." She later starred as country singer Juliette Barnes on "Nashville," earning two Golden Globe nominations, and appeared as Kirby Reed in the "Scream" franchise.
WATCH: NEW DETAILS SURFACE SURROUNDING HAYDEN PANETTIERE'S DEATH

Her death came a little more than three years after her younger brother, Jansen Panettiere, died in 2023 at age 28 from an enlarged heart coupled with aortic valve complications. Panettiere had spoken openly about the profound grief she experienced after his death.
Despite the pain Chatwin said he witnessed, his description of how he hopes Panettiere will be remembered was simple.
"She was a unicorn."
And when asked what Panettiere had told him about returning to acting and what she wanted to do next, Chatwin said her focus wasn't on another role or career milestone.

"I think the only focus was to be happy," he said.

title: Major brain changes that occur around age 50 could impact dementia risk
summary: Microglia decline after age 50 as inflammatory blood-derived immune cells infiltrate the hippocampus, potentially driving neuroinflammation and dementia.
story: Dr. Daniel Amen — psychiatrist, brain imaging specialist and founder of Amen Clinics in California — says this quick, 15-second method can help calm the body and mind.
The brain may undergo a notable shift at midlife, as new research suggests that its protective immune cells begin to decline and are increasingly replaced by inflammatory cells at around age 50.

Researchers from the University of California, San Diego; New York Genome Center; and University of California, Irvine, found that these brain changes may help explain why aging increases the chances of neuroinflammation and neurodegenerative disease, including dementia.

The study analyzed postmortem tissue from the hippocampus – the portion of the brain that is responsible for learning and memory – in 40 neurologically healthy adults, ranging from 20 to 95 years of age.
THE 'AGE' OF YOUR BLOOD COULD PREDICT DEMENTIA RISK, NEW STUDY SUGGESTS

"The most striking change was that after about age 50, the brain’s resident immune cells, called microglia, appear to be increasingly replaced by immune cells that enter from the bloodstream," first author Nathan Zemke, Ph.D., principal investigator at the UC San Diego Center for Epigenomics, told Fox News Digital.
"Microglia normally protect the brain by clearing debris and responding to injury, but the incoming cells carry stronger inflammatory signals."

The brain may undergo a notable shift at midlife, as new research suggests that its protective immune cells begin to decline and are increasingly replaced by inflammatory cells at around age 50. (iStock)
The researchers believe this shift may contribute to chronic inflammation linked to cognitive decline and neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer’s.

They also noted the deterioration of cells involved in maintaining the blood-brain barrier – the protective filter that helps keep harmful substances out of the brain – as well as widespread changes in DNA and gene activity.
'LONGEVITY GENE' MAY PROTECT THE BRAIN FROM ALZHEIMER'S BY BOOSTING DNA REPAIR, STUDY FINDS

One of the most exciting implications of the study, according to Zemke, is that the replacement immune cells originate in the blood, which means they are more accessible than cells already deep inside the brain.

"It may eventually be possible to modify blood-derived immune cells so that they are more protective and less inflammatory when in the brain," he said. "That could provide an entirely new way to approach Alzheimer’s and other neurological diseases without having to directly manipulate cells within the central nervous system."
Researchers found that these brain changes may help explain why aging increases the chances of neuroinflammation and neurodegenerative disease, including dementia. (iStock)

Although these findings are still in early stages, Zemke said, gaining a better understanding of why this immune-cell replacement happens – and why it happens earlier in some people than others – could lead to new strategies for preserving brain health during aging.
The study’s chief limitation is that it studied human brain tissue collected postmortem from different individuals across the adult lifespan, the researchers noted.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"That allows us to identify strong age-related patterns, but it cannot directly show how the same person’s brain changes over decades or prove that a particular cellular change causes cognitive decline or Alzheimer’s disease," Zemke said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"We also do not yet know what triggers the influx of blood-derived immune cells into the brain. Determining whether changes in the blood-brain barrier, inflammation, genetics, lifestyle or other factors initiate this process will be an important next step."
The timing and extent of the brain changes varied considerably between individuals, suggesting that brain aging is not necessarily a fixed process that happens identically in everyone. (iStock)
The researcher emphasized, however, that he would not recommend that people make any specific medical or lifestyle changes based on this study alone.
"These findings are primarily about understanding the biology of brain aging and identifying new directions for prevention and treatment," he said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The timing and extent of the brain changes varied considerably between individuals, suggesting that brain aging is not necessarily a fixed process that happens identically in everyone.
"The next challenge is to understand what drives that variation and whether some of those factors can be modified," Zemke added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The study also included a small sample of just 40 people and examined tissue only from the hippocampus, meaning the findings may not reflect immune changes throughout the entire brain.
The study, which was funded by the National Institutes of Health, was published in the journal Science.

title: Anti-aging supplements taken by millions may undermine cancer treatment, study warns
summary: Popular NAD+-boosting supplements like NMN and nicotinamide riboside may shield pancreatic cancer cells from chemotherapy, a new study warns.
story: Family medicine physician Dr. Jessica Gray details a new experimental pancreatic cancer vaccine showing promise in its first human trial. The vaccine, targeting the KRAS mutation, generated an immune response in 90% of high-risk patients. Dr. Gray discusses the 5-7 year timeline for public availability and emphasizes why pancreatic cancer is so deadly, highlighting advances in cancer treatments.
Over-the-counter anti-aging supplements taken by millions of Americans to boost energy and lessen the side effects of chemotherapy may actually impair cancer treatments, a new study suggests.

Researchers at the Case Western Reserve University School of Medicine found that popular vitamin B3 derivatives – including nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), nicotinamide riboside (NR) and nicotinamide (NAM) – could help cancer cells survive chemotherapy.
Those compounds are used by the body to produce NAD+, a molecule that helps cells generate energy and repair damage.
IV THERAPY AND SUPPLEMENTS UNDER SCRUTINY AS EXPERTS WARN OF POTENTIAL SIDE EFFECTS

The study, published in the journal Cancer Letters, examined how these supplements interact with treatments for pancreatic cancer, a particularly deadly form of the disease with a 13% five-year survival rate, according to the American Cancer Society.
Over-the-counter vitamin B3 derivatives, specifically NMN, NR and NAM, could help pancreatic cancer cells survive chemotherapy treatment, the study suggests. (iStock)

While boosting NAD+ levels through dietary supplements can offer health benefits to non-cancerous cells, pancreatic cancer cells may exploit the extra resources to repair damage caused by chemotherapy and avoid cell death, the researchers found.

In both laboratory settings and animal models, the supplements shielded cancer cells against three common chemotherapy drugs: oxaliplatin, 5-fluorouracil and gemcitabine. As a result, tumors survived chemotherapy doses that typically would prove fatal to them.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Our findings highlight a potentially concerning role for NAD+-boosting supplements in the context of active cancer, especially when used in conjunction with chemotherapy," said study lead Jordan Winter, a professor at Case Western Reserve School of Medicine and co-leader of the developmental therapeutics program at the Case Comprehensive Cancer Center, in the press release.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Our discovery is a call to action for the medical community."

The study notes that these B3 derivatives are not considered dangerous for healthy individuals using them for general wellness. However, the risk becomes significant for patients currently undergoing active cancer therapy.
Boosting NAD+ levels provides extra energy to cancer cells, allowing them to repair DNA damage caused by chemotherapy. (iStock)
"This research is a critical reminder that ‘natural’ doesn’t always mean safe, especially in the complex biology of cancer treatment," Winter added.

In light of the findings, the research team recommends that oncology teams begin routinely screening patients for supplement use. They also called for more studies into how NAD+ precursors interact with cancer therapies.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Winter urged patients currently in treatment to consult their oncologists before taking any over-the-counter supplements.
Because the study relied on laboratory cell cultures and animal models, the findings may not directly translate to how human patients process these supplements during treatment, the team noted.

The findings indicate these supplements are not inherently dangerous for healthy individuals using them for general anti-aging or wellness, but pose serious risks when taken during active chemotherapy. (iStock)
Additionally, the research focused exclusively on pancreatic cancer, meaning the supplements may not have the same effect on chemotherapy for other cancer types or with different drug combinations.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The study also only evaluated short-term cellular responses under controlled laboratory conditions and not human clinical trials, so it remains unclear how these supplements could affect cancer patients over time.
Fox News Digital reached out to multiple NAD+ supplement manufacturers for comment.
